title: Balancing the Scales of Justice: Public Defender and District Attorney Value-Added
affiliations: Brown University

detail.title: Balancing the Scales of Justice: Public Defender and District Attorney Value-Added
detail.abstract: The adversarial nature of the American criminal justice system presumes that competition between public defenders (PDs) and district attorneys (DAs) yields fair outcomes, yet disparities in attorney skill may distort this process. This paper exploits the random assignment of attorneys in 15 years of administrative data from Bexar County, Texas, to estimate the value-added of attorneys on case outcomes. Attorney value-added has large effects on the probability of incarceration which are symmetric and additive such that having an above median DA (PD) and a below median PD (DA) increases (decreases) the probability of incarceration by approximately 10 percentage points. When attorneys have equal value-added, their effects cancel out, but imbalances in attorney value-added generate substantial variation in case outcomes. Even when PD and DA value-added are balanced, differences in attorney value-added affect the composition of released defendants: higher value-added pairs are more likely to release younger, first-time defendants, who subsequently exhibit higher rates of recidivism.

title: A Tale of the Financial Inclusion-Growth Nexus and the Degree of Financial Inclusion: A Dynamic Panel Approach on Selected Developing Countries
affiliations: East West University, East West University and University of Otago

detail.title: A Tale of the Financial Inclusion-Growth Nexus and the Degree of Financial Inclusion: A Dynamic Panel Approach on Selected Developing Countries

keywords: Panel Fixed Effect Instrumental Variable (FEIV) Method

detail.abstract:
Purpose

This study aims to examine the impact of financial inclusion on per capita gross domestic product (GDP) at varying degrees of financial inclusion for a sample of 76 developing countries between 2011 and 2017. To evaluate the heterogeneous impact, this paper constructs the multi-dimension index of financial inclusion to classify sample countries into two sub-samples in terms of the value of FIID, taking account of three dimensions of financial inclusion: access, usage and availability.

Design/methodology/approach

This study attempts to identify the presence of reverse causality and long-run relationship between financial inclusion and economic growth by using the Granger causality test (Wald test) and three alternative panel cointegration tests (Kao Test, Pedroni Test, Westerlund Test) respectively. Because of the existence of the bi-directional causality between financial inclusion and per capita GDP, this study uses a fixed effect instrumental variable model with lagged dependent variable to get unbiased estimators from the panel regressions for sample countries.

Findings

This paper finds a strong positive impact of financial inclusion on per capita GDP growth in sample developing countries, controlling for labor market structure, financial institutions’ efficacy, infrastructural and governance issues. This study suggests that economic growth will be high in developing economies with a higher level of financial inclusion; however, the positive impact for two sub-samples countries (low and medium level of inclusion and high level of inclusion) are heterogeneous. The estimated result explains that a 1% increase in the financial inclusion index leads to a 0.0153% point increase in the per capita GDP for the countries with a low and medium level of financial inclusion, while this positive impact is significantly higher, 0.0794% point for countries with the high level of financial inclusion. This study also suggests that the higher concentration in the financial market by few agents and the lower level of governance may have an adverse impact on economic growth for the economies with a low and medium level of financial inclusion.

Originality/value

This study is an original study that contributes to the research gap by explaining the heterogeneous impact of financial inclusion on economic growth at varying degrees of inclusion in the two sub-sample countries. Moreover, this study posits greater appeal as it explores the issue using the sample of only developing economies.

title: The Spatial Inflation Wedge: One Size Fits None in the U.S. Economy
affiliations: Florida International University (FIU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Spatial Inflation Wedge: One Size Fits None in the U.S. Economy
detail.abstract: We estimate optimal inflation targets for United States cities by exploiting structural trends in relative prices, extending the sufficient statistic framework for optimal inflation to the spatial dimension. Using a comprehensive panel of micro-price data derived from the Cost of Living Index (COLI) covering 323 U.S. urban areas from 1990 to 2023, we document a massive structural divergence in efficient relative prices. We find that relative prices in lagging regions (particularly in the Midwest and South) exhibit a secular decline, while relative prices in booming regions (such as the coastal West) exhibit a secular rise. Driven mostly by the non-tradable sector, this divergence creates a spatial inflation wedge of approximately 2.5 percentage points. While booming cities require an inflation rate approximately 1.0 percentage point lower than the national average to minimize relative price distortions, lagging cities require a rate roughly 1.5 percentage points higher than the average. Consequently, having a single national inflation target acts as a contractionary shock to the Rust Belt, forcing relative price adjustments to occur via nominal stagnation, while simultaneously providing an inflationary subsidy to the Coasts. Our results suggest that optimal monetary policy in a heterogeneous national economy must account for the spatial distribution of relative price trends.

title: From Tweets to Transactions: High-Frequency Inflation Expectations, Consumption, and Stock Returns
affiliations: Frankfurt School of Finance & Management, , Frankfurt School of Finance & Management and Frankfurt School of Finance & Management

detail.title: From Tweets to Transactions: High-Frequency Inflation Expectations, Consumption, and Stock Returns
detail.abstract:
Using modern natural language processing, we construct a high-frequency inflation expectations
index from German-language tweets. This index closely tracks realized inflation and aligns even more closely with household survey expectations. It also improves short-run forecasts relative to standard benchmarks. In response to monetary policy tightening, the index declines within about a week, with the effects concentrated in tweets by private individuals and during the recent period of elevated inflation. Using 117 million online transactions from German retailers, we show that higher inflation expectations are followed by lower household spending on discretionary goods. By linking these shifts in demand to stock returns, we find that, during periods of elevated inflation, firms operating in discretionary sectors experience significantly lower stock returns when inflation expectations rise. Thus, our Twitter-based index provides market participants and policymakers with a timely tool to monitor inflation sentiment and its economic consequences.

title: Continuous Regime-Dependence in Inflation Dynamics: A Structural Unification of the Borio and SRDB Frameworks
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Continuous Regime-Dependence in Inflation Dynamics: A Structural Unification of the Borio and SRDB Frameworks
detail.abstract: Recent literature, notably Borio (2017, 2021), posits that inflation dynamics alternate between a "supply-push" regime decoupled from domestic slack and a "demand-pull" regime driven by the financial cycle. This paper integrates this hypothesis into the Systemic Risk of Doing Business (SRDB) framework, demonstrating that Borio's discrete regimes emerge as asymptotic boundary cases of a continuous, micro-founded risk pricing kernel. Using a state-space Kalman filter on data from 15 economies (1990-2024), we validate the model against standard benchmarks. In a direct forecasting horse race, the continuous SRDB weighting scheme outperforms not only standard Phillips Curves and discrete regimeswitching heuristics but also Time-Varying Parameter (TVP) models and Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA). By explicitly linking risk weights to observable cycle indicators, the SRDB model reduces out-of-sample RMSE by 44% during crisis transitions where statistical drift models typically lag.

title: Canada as a Nuclear Governance State: Export Controls, Safeguards, and the Architecture of International Nuclear Law
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Canada as a Nuclear Governance State: Export Controls, Safeguards, and the Architecture of International Nuclear Law

keywords: Atomic energy treaties and compliance; Non-proliferation and safeguards law; Canadian foreign and security policy; Global nuclear commerce; Comparative nuclear governance; International energy law

detail.abstract:
International nuclear law is commonly understood through formal treaty frameworks such as the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and the institutional role of the International Atomic Energy Agency. This paper argues that such treaty-centric accounts overlook a critical dimension of contemporary nuclear governance: the regulatory practices of supplier states. Using Canada as a case study, the paper advances the concept of the “nuclear governance state” to describe how domestic export control regimes, licensing discretion, and safeguards implementation operate as de facto sources of international nuclear law.

Through a doctrinal and institutional analysis of Canada’s nuclear export control framework, including the Nuclear Safety and Control Act, the Export and Import Permits Act, and the regulatory authority of the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, the paper demonstrates how international non-proliferation norms are operationalized through domestic administrative decision-making. Canadian licensing practices, end-use conditions, verification requirements, and revocation powers translate abstract treaty obligations into enforceable governance mechanisms that shape the conduct of importing states beyond formal legal commitments.

By situating Canadian practice within comparative supplier-state governance, including Australia and the United States, the paper shows how export controls function not merely as compliance tools but as instruments of norm creation and institutional trust-building. It concludes that the future development of international nuclear law will depend less on new treaties and more on the regulatory architecture of responsible supplier states. This reconceptualization has broader implications for international law, administrative governance, and the regulation of dual-use commodities in an era of energy transition and geopolitical instability.

title: The Emerging Market for Intelligence: Pricing, Supply, and Demand for LLMs
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, Boston University, Microsoft Corp. and Microsoft Corporation

detail.title: The Emerging Market for Intelligence: Pricing, Supply, and Demand for LLMs

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We document six facts about the structure and dynamics of the LLM market using API usage data from OpenRouter and Microsoft Azure. First, we show rapid growth in the number of models, creators, and inference providers, driven by open-source entrants. Second, we show price declines and persistent price heterogeneity across and within intelligence tiers, with open-source models being 90% cheaper than comparable closed-source models of the same intelligence. Third, we document market dynamism, with frequent turnover among leading models and creators. Fourth, we present evidence of horizontal and vertical differentiation, with no single model dominating across use cases, and demand for intelligence varying widely across applications. Fifth, we estimate preliminary short-run price elasticities just above one, suggesting limited scope for Jevons-Paradox effects. Finally, we show that although the share of firms that use multiple models increased over time, most firms concentrate their use on a single model, consistent with experimentation rather than persistent reliance on multiple models.

title: National Innovation Capability Enablers and Outcomes, Corruption, and Progression to Higher Stages of CBDC Adoption
affiliations: Hamline University

detail.title: National Innovation Capability Enablers and Outcomes, Corruption, and Progression to Higher Stages of CBDC Adoption
detail.abstract:
Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) have garnered much interest from scholars, practitioners, and policymakers alike. A survey of the literature that has explored a country’s characteristics as determinants of its CBDC adoption suggests a multifaceted landscape shaped by a confluence of political, legal, economic, financial, technological, social, and cultural factors. However, less is known about the role that the national system of innovation (NSI) characteristics may play in the adoption of a CBDC. To fill this research gap, this dissertation explored how five national innovation capability enablers (i.e., institutions, human research and capital, infrastructure, market sophistication, and business sophistication) and two national innovation capability outcomes (i.e., knowledge and technology outputs and creative outputs) influenced a country’s advancement to higher stages of CBDC adoption. Further, it examined the role that corruption—defined as the abuse of entrusted power (or public office) for private gain—played as a moderator, i.e., whether it strengthened or weakened the impact of the five national innovation enablers and the two national innovation outcomes on a country’s progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption, respectively.

Analyzing a unique dataset compiling archival data gathered from the CBDC Tracker, Global Innovation Index, Global Governance Indicators, Corruption Perceptions Index, and Worldwide Corruption Index by employing ordered logistic regression, the study in this dissertation found that none of the five national innovation capability enablers—institutions, human capital and research, infrastructure, market sophistication, and business sophistication—had statistically significant positive impact on a country’s progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption. However, creative outputs—one of the two national innovation capability outcomes—were found to have statistically significant positive impact on a country’s progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption, while the other national innovation capability outcomes (i.e., knowledge and technology outputs) did not. Further, corruption was found to play a moderating role in the case of two national innovation capability enablers. Corruption positively moderated the relationship between institutions and a country’s progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption, whereas corruption negatively moderated the relationship between market sophistication and a country’s progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption. In other words, the positive relationship between institutions and a country’s progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption was stronger in countries with lower levels of corruption than in those with higher levels of corruption, whereas the positive relationship between market sophistication and a country’s progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption was stronger in countries with higher levels of corruption than in those with lower levels of corruption.

detail.abstract:
Why do some entrepreneurs drive economic growth while others do not? This piece discusses new work that studies entrepreneurs using a comprehensive dataset from Denmark. We study who becomes an entrepreneur, along with their hiring and business decisions, and find that a distinct minority are “transformative.” These individuals, who generate disproportionate productivity gains, tend to have high IQ scores, be well-educated, and hire technical (R&D) workers. The data support the idea of productivity growth being driven by the symbiotic relationship between transformative entrepreneurs and R&D workers. For policymakers, the lesson is that when an economy has more R&D workers and transformative entrepreneurs, they sustain higher long-run productivity growth.

title: Lack of Effective Recycling of LFP Batteries

detail.title: Lack of Effective Recycling of LFP Batteries
detail.abstract: Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries have rapidly expanded their share of the global EV and stationary storage market, reaching more than 40–50% of total volume in 2024–2025. However, unlike nickel- and cobalt-rich chemistries, LFP contains low-value materials, making traditional recycling methods—pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy—economically and environmentally inefficient. These legacy processes involve high energy consumption, significant chemical waste, lithium losses, and recovery pathways that fail to return cathode materials to a reusable state. As LFP adoption accelerates, this gap creates a growing environmental risk and a missed economic opportunity across national supply chains. MaxAh addresses this challenge through industrial-scale direct recycling, a regeneration-based approach that preserves the crystal structure of LFP cathodes and enables relithiation with minimal processing. Pilot studies demonstrate 40–60% lower energy consumption, 85–95% active material recovery, and substantially reduced CO₂ emissions compared with conventional methods. By recovering high-quality cathode-active material (CAM) and graphite anodes suitable for direct reuse, the technology enables a cost-effective and low-waste circular pathway for LFP batteries. This work highlights the strategic importance of direct recycling for building resilient battery supply chains, reducing dependence on primary extraction, and enabling economically viable, low-carbon recovery of LFP materials at scale.

title: One Instrument, Many Treatments: Instrumental Variables Identification of Multiple Causal Effects
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Department of Economics and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics

detail.title: One Instrument, Many Treatments: Instrumental Variables Identification of Multiple Causal Effects

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Many instrumental variables applications specify a single Bernoulli treatment. But instruments may change outcomes through multiple pathways or by varying treatment intensity. Lottery instruments that boost charter school enrollment, for instance, may affect outcomes by lengthening time enrolled in a charter school and by moving students between charter schools of different types. We analyze the identification problem such scenarios present in a framework that generalizes the always-taker/never-taker/complier partition of treatment response types to cover a wide range of multinomial and ordered treatments with heterogenous potential outcomes. This framework yields novel estimators in which a single randomly assigned instrument identifies (i) causal effects averaged over complier types and (ii) a causal conditional expectation function that captures effects for each element in a set of response types. Three empirical applications demonstrate the utility of these results. The first extends an earlier analysis of the Head Start Impact Study allowing for multiple fallbacks. The second examines two causal channels for the impact of post-secondary financial aid on degree completion. The third estimates effects of additional births (an ordered treatment) on mothers’ earnings.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Possible Effects of the Tripartite Declaration (21 October 2020) on the Economic and Political Relations of the Türkiye Azerbaijan and Armenia
affiliations: Turkish Ministry of Trade and Necmettin Erbakan University

detail.title: Possible Effects of the Tripartite Declaration (21 October 2020) on the Economic and Political Relations of the Türkiye Azerbaijan and Armenia
detail.abstract: After the independence of Azerbaijan and Armenia, the Karabakh problem ceased to be an internal problem of the USSR and transformed into a regional and even a global problem. The South Caucasus has gained importance in world geopolitics since the 1990s due to the oil and natural gas transportation lines. Armenia, which has appeared to be an unstable country due to the Karabakh conflict, has not benefited from any regional project. Moreover, Türkiye has restricted transportation opportunities in Armenia. Because of the war with Azerbaijan. Armenia has become an isolated country. Thus, the government has become largely dependent on Russia politically and economically. Also, the war has almost caused the country's economy to the verge of bankruptcy. The Tripartite Declaration concluded between Russia, Azerbaijan, and Armenia on November 10, 2020, has brought collaboration opportunities for these countries and Türkiye. It has been concluded that increasing economic cooperation will also contribute to solving the countries' political problems. Additionally, the scope of economic diplomacy, particularly Türkiye's application of soft power elements, can positively affect Armenian public opinion and relations between the two countries.

title: The Politics of Climate Hope and Despair

detail.title: The Politics of Climate Hope and Despair
detail.abstract:
Two of the modern world’s greatest challenges are more intertwined than we recognize: the risk of global upheaval from climate change and the threat to democracy from the consistent erosion of our institutions, particularly by political polarization, the internet, and social media. 

David Spence’s powerful book, Climate of Contempt: How to Rescue the U.S. Energy Transition from Voter Partisanship, unpacks and explains this mutual, if troubling, relationship. Deftly blending a mastery of energy law and political science, Spence draws on a staggering array of both real-world examples and the full range of social science to show not just why these dual threats matter but how they are deeply connected. Even though the U.S. electorate wants climate legislation, increasing partisanship has stalled congressional action. Why?

This review overviews Spence's book, explains its successes, and then explores a triad of questions that inevitably arise from a close consideration of these vital topics.

title: 2025 Japan's Stewardship Code
affiliations: University College London - Faculty of Laws

detail.title: 2025 Japan's Stewardship Code

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming, Revue Trimestrielle de Droit Financier (Corporate Finance and Capital Markets Law Review, RTDF), N°4-2025.

detail.abstract:
Japan's Stewardship Code was established in 2014 amid structural changes in Japan's capital markets. Alongside the 2015 Corporate Governance Code and several other "market soft laws" issued by organisations such as the Tokyo Stock Exchange, it has significantly promoted the growth of investor activism in Japan.

Despite lacking legal enforceability, these soft laws have a significant influence, which could largely be attributed to activist investors effectively compelling companies to implement them. The 2017 revision of the Stewardship Code, which recommended the individual disclosure of institutional investors' voting outcomes, is also considered to have substantially fueled the recent surge in investor activism in Japan. 

The 2025 revision, by recommending collaborative engagement, aims to advance investor activism to a further stage. Simultaneously, by enhancing transparency regarding beneficial shareholders, it seeks to foster healthy engagement between investors and companies. It is noted that various issues remain on both the investor and corporate sides regarding the nature of engagement, and these constitute concrete challenges for the future. 

A key characteristic of Japan's Stewardship Code is that it has explicitly stated the objective of "promoting sustainable corporate growth" since its inception. In light of the significant increase in investor activism, achieving this objective will be the most critical challenge going forward. While discussions often focus on how investor-led initiatives can promote "sustainable corporate growth", it is also important to recognise that company law in many jurisdictions effectively grants directors and other officers broad discretion over corporate activities. Consequently, renewed attention should be given to the potential for companies to take the lead in undertaking socially responsible activities through engagement with investors.

title: Learning About the Macroeconomy Through Mortgages: Evidence from a Natural Experiment

detail.title: Learning About the Macroeconomy Through Mortgages: Evidence from a Natural Experiment

declarations.funderStatement: I have received data funding from the University of Helsinki and Yrjö Jahnsson Foundation.

detail.abstract: Household beliefs about the macroeconomy play a central role in the transmission of monetary policy. I study how adjustable-rate mortgages shape the effect of rising interest rates on household beliefs, using detailed Finnish data that link administrative mortgage records with survey-based beliefs. Exploiting the increase in market rates and the variation in the timing of mortgage payment adjustments, I find that mortgage borrowers update their macroeconomic beliefs more than homeowners without mortgages and renters. After rates rise, mortgage borrowers become more pessimistic about general borrowing conditions and predict lower inflation than homeowners without mortgages and renters, even though all groups face the same macroeconomic environment. These shifts are driven by two complementary mechanisms: an attention-based mechanism, where holding a mortgage creates stronger incentives to follow macroeconomic developments, and an experience-based mechanism, where households extrapolate from their own higher mortgage payments to form beliefs about the general borrowing environment. As a result of the increase in interest rates, mortgage borrowers' inflation forecasts become more accurate relative to homeowners without mortgages and renters, suggesting that adjustable-rate loans are an important channel for monetary policy transmission and can serve as an information channel for households.

title: Quantitatively restricted international emissions trading agreements under general equilibrium effects
affiliations: Beihang University (BUAA) and Beihang University (BUAA)

detail.title: Quantitatively restricted international emissions trading agreements under general equilibrium effects
detail.abstract: International emissions trading (IET) appears attractive for saving global abatement costs and achieving mutual benefits. However, this ideal outcome can only be established in a partial equilibrium setting with no economic friction. As argued by previous studies, unrestricted IET (i.e. full linkage between permit markets) is not necessarily beneficial for individual jurisdictions due to the presence of general equilibrium (GE) effects. In such a context, we investigate whether it is possible for two countries to cooperate through a quantitatively restricted IET agreement and, if so, how the equilibrium trading volume is determined and its welfare implications. Using a tractable two-country analytical model, we formally characterize the scope of possible trading volumes as the feasible Pareto-efficient set, and the equilibrium trading volume as the Nash bargaining solution of bilateral negotiation. To illustrate our theoretical thinking, we simulate two hypothetical IET cases using a tailored multi-region computable general equilibrium model, which flexibly captures three kinds of GE effects, namely tax interaction, terms-of-trade and labor market distortion. We find that the equilibrium trading volume under restricted IET is critically dependent on assumptions of GE effects and the inter-jurisdictional trading price. This trading volume could even lead to higher system welfare than unrestricted IET when two sides’ GE effects are located in certain ranges. We conclude that restricted IET can serve as an economically viable option for global climate cooperation, particularly when distortive GE effects prevail.

detail.abstract: Nigeria's 2025 tax codification is the most consequential rewrite of federal tax rules in decades. Beyond structural consolidation, the new Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 and the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 establish a coherent framework of tax incentives to stimulate investment, formalization, innovation and exports, while building stronger safeguards against abuse. This article identifies and analyses the incentive architecture income-tax exemptions and deductions, the new Economic Development Tax Credit regime for priority sectors, VAT and stamp duty exemptions, business restructuring reliefs, and compliance facilitation for small businesses and evaluates their likely impact on firm behavior and state revenues. It argues that the 2025 regime improves legal clarity, embeds horizontality (open, rules based access), integrates administrative transparency (notably through Priority Company and Incentive Return reporting), and strengthens anti-avoidance levers. It concludes with implementation priorities to ensure incentive value for money, including rigorous certificate governance, targeted guidance, and data-driven audits.

title: National hydrogen strategies: Policy impacts and adoption drivers
affiliations: University of Adelaide, University of Adelaide and University of Adelaide

detail.title: National hydrogen strategies: Policy impacts and adoption drivers
detail.abstract: The global transition to low-carbon energy has led many countries to adopt national hydrogen strategies, yet their policy impacts and adoption drivers remain poorly understood. This paper investigates these issues using panel data for 49 countries from 2010 to 2023. Policy impacts are assessed via a staggered difference-in-differences framework, while the determinants of adoption are analysed using a fixed-effects linear probability model. We find that adoption is associated with a sustained and economically significant increase in public hydrogen R&D spending, signalling credible government commitment, and a smaller rise in carbon capture, utilisation, and storage (CCUS) R&D, reflecting continued support for fossil-fuel-linked technologies. No short-run reduction in industrial process emissions is observed, suggesting that decarbonisation effects materialise gradually. Turning to the determinants of adoption, within-country growth in renewable electricity generation emerges as the strongest predictor of adoption, highlighting the interdependence between renewable expansion and hydrogen policy formation, while macroeconomic and political factors appear largely insignificant. These results shed light on the effectiveness and determinants of national hydrogen strategies in the global energy transition.

title: Nuclear power expansion and renewable generation curtailment in Korea - the role of distributed storage
affiliations: , Lehigh University and Cornell University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Nuclear power expansion and renewable generation curtailment in Korea - the role of distributed storage
detail.abstract: The Korean government has set an ambitious plan to address climate change by relying more on the generation of electricity from nuclear power and variable renewable energy sources (VRES) and less on fossil units.  This plan raises the question of how the inherent uncertainty of VRES should be mitigated.  Unlike the generation from fossil units, particularly natural gas turbines, nuclear units are relatively inflexible and are unable to offset the variability of VRES effectively.  Without additional resources, it will be inevitable that some of the potential generation from VRES will have to be curtailed at certain times.  Substantial curtailments of VRES have occurred regularly in regions of the US, like California, and in countries, like Germany.  A sensible solution to this predicament is to make load more responsive to supply by adding distributed storage capacity.  An empirical analysis of the Korean energy plan is conducted to evaluate the potential contribution of electric vehicles (EV) to reducing curtailments of VRES.  The results show that the ``smart charging'' of EVs has only a modest effect on curtailments.  In contrast, providing EVs with vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capabilities has a substantial effect because the full capacity of the batteries can be used.  The overall conclusion is that having distributed storage capacity that responds to real-time prices is an effective way to accommodate VRES and avoid curtailments.  The question remains of what types of storage, for example  batteries or thermal storage, are best given the composition of the load in Korea.

title: The crisis that a U.S. debt default would unleash
affiliations: Handong Global University

detail.title: The crisis that a U.S. debt default would unleash

detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes the potential economic and financial consequences of a U.S. debt default and argues that the greater long-term risk lies not in default itself but in the country’s rapidly expanding fiscal imbalance. While a technical default could trigger severe but temporary market disruptions—such as a sharp decline in equity prices, higher risk premiums, and a downgrade of U.S. sovereign credit—the Federal Reserve possesses tools to stabilize markets by accepting defaulted securities as collateral and ensuring liquidity. Historical precedent also suggests that U.S. political actors ultimately avoid crossing the default threshold.

However, the paper highlights that America’s escalating fiscal deficits and rising interest-burden ratio represent a deeper structural threat. Federal debt relative to GDP is projected to exceed 118% within a decade, driven by demographic pressures, entitlement spending, and insufficient revenue growth. With high interest rates amplifying borrowing costs, the U.S. faces a long-run solvency challenge that the debt ceiling mechanism fails to address. The report concludes that bipartisan political gridlock—not excessive borrowing alone—prevents meaningful fiscal reform, making the nation’s chronic deficit trajectory a more plausible catalyst for future economic instability than a short-term default event.

title: When Trade Turns Strategic: Lessons from Fourteen Trade Wars for U.S.-China Strategic Competition
affiliations: Harvard University

detail.title: When Trade Turns Strategic: Lessons from Fourteen Trade Wars for U.S.-China Strategic Competition
detail.abstract: Trade is both an economic and a strategic instrument. Symmetric interdependence and rough power parity draw it toward its economic dimension and lower escalation risk; by contrast, asymmetric interdependence and power imbalances pull it toward a strategic role, raising that risk by lowering the costs and increasing the expected returns of coercion. Geopolitical competition also reinforces the strategic role of trade. A particular configuration of such rivalry arises when a hegemon is challenged by a rising power, prompting both sides to hedge against interdependence. This paper terms this dynamic the "Trade Thucydides Trap"; after eight decades of Pax Americana, its preconditions are present in today's U.S-China competition. To study the strategic deployment of trade, this paper reviews fourteen great-power trade conflicts (17th century-1980s), about half of which escalated into open conflict, and then focuses on the eight cases most analogous to the contemporary U.S.-China competition. Translating history into assessment, the paper builds a U.S.-China scorecard and introduces a Strategic Leverage Ratio. Results show broad bilateral parity, and that U.S. leverage peaked in the mid-1990s and has declined since, implying limited coercive capacity over Beijing.

title: Inaction Inertia in Economic Decision Making: The Role of Reference Points
affiliations: HSE University

detail.title: Inaction Inertia in Economic Decision Making: The Role of Reference Points
detail.abstract: The study explores a psychological phenomenon of inaction inertia-avoiding action after missing a more favourable opportunity. Unlike action inertia (e.g.,sunk costs effect), inaction inertia has been less studied, particularly in economic contexts. Considering the reference dependent nature of the phenomenon, I build on the work of Kőszegi and Rabin (2006) to examine how past experiences and expectations of future price changes influence consumer decision making. Key findings from the model include: 1) anchoring by missed opportunities: consumers perceive current offers as less attractive if they are aware of a better deal previously missed; 2) expectations of future discounts reduce the likelihood of immediate purchases. An experiment involving 148 participants supports the first prediction, however, no evidence for the second prediction is found. The study highlights the role of loss aversion and regret avoidance in driving inaction inertia. Practical implications suggest that marketers should consider potential post-promotional dips.

title: Globalization Of Outflow Turkish Investment: The Change of Geographical Differentiation and the Investment Reasons

detail.abstract: After Turkey's liberalization of capital movements in the 1980s, the FDI of Turkish firms began to increase. The change in the Decision No. 32 on the Protection of the Value of Turkish Currency in 1989, the customs union agreement in 1995, and the disintegration of the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia in the same years created an important opportunity for Turkish companies. Turkish companies, mainly SMEs, initially made investments in countries located in close geographies such as the Balkans, Central Asia and the Caucasus, especially for cost advantage and access to resources. The EU membership negotiations, which started in 2005, accelerated the flow of foreign investment into the country, which created competitive pressure. Turkey's relatively comfortable recovery from the 2008 global crisis created new opportunities for Turkish companies to invest abroad. Especially family holdings have started to invest in developed regions such as Western Europe and North America for strategic purposes such as access to new technology. Africa and Asia-Pacific regions have been regions where investments have increased recently. With these developments, Turkey’s FDI (outflow) has started to change significantly from regional to global.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a complete quantitative workflow for designing, validating, and stresstesting short-horizon cryptocurrency strategies. The framework integrates volatility-regime detection via KNN classification, MFE/MAE ratio modeling with gradient boosting, probability calibration via Platt scaling, and a production-grade execution engine with FTMO-style Monte Carlo validation. Crucially, the strategy maintains robust out-of-sample performance with 91.9% pass rate preservation and identical Sharpe characteristics, demonstrating a real statistical edge free from data leakage or overfitting within the studied market and horizon.

detail.abstract: We leverage Becker's time allocation theory to examine consumer demand and market competition for time-intensive goods. The Beckerian model predicts higher diversion ratios for goods with substantial time shares and those with high time costs relative to monetary prices. Applying this model to data from two field experiments, we analyze demand for Facebook and Instagram, focusing on substitution patterns across online activities and offline time use. Our findings indicate that users exhibit low elasticity to ad load, the primary user cost, and that time shares and time costs significantly influence diversion ratios. We explore the implications for user costs and benefits on these platforms and assess the potential impact of a Federal Trade Commission-proposed de-merger of Facebook and Instagram.

title: It Starts Early! Male-Dominated Classes and Girls' Bullying

detail.title: It Starts Early! Male-Dominated Classes and Girls' Bullying

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Bullying is a widespread form of aggression that emerges early in childhood and is common in school settings. Using Italian data from the National Institute for the Evaluation of Education and Training (INVALSI) on primary school students, we document gender differences in self-reported bullying, both as victims and perpetrators, across multiple dimensions. Bullying is more prevalent among boys on both fronts. Exploiting the quasi-random allocation of students to classes within schools, we show that a higher share of boys increases reported victimization among girls, particularly in forms such as mockery and verbal insults. These effects are associated with lower well-being among girls. The findings point to a spillover of violence from boys to girls as the share of male peers increases, highlighting the role of classroom gender composition in shaping early peer interactions and the need for caution when managing gender imbalances in elementary education.

detail.abstract: In 2025, statutory tariff rates on U.S. imports rose to levels not seen in over one hundred years. What are the implications for prices? On the one hand, shipping lags, exemptions, and enforcement gaps have kept the actual implemented rates at only half of the statutory rates, moderating the tariffs' impact. On the other hand, tariff pass-through to U.S. import prices is almost 100 percent, so the United States is bearing a large share of the costs. We study the incidence of the 2018-2019 and 2025 U.S. tariffs and discuss implications for U.S. sourcing, domestic manufacturing costs, and the dollar.

title: Weighting the H-1B Lottery: Implications for Worker and Diversity and Employment Concentration
affiliations: Colgate University

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: The H-1B program allows firms in the United States to temporarily hire foreign workers in specialty occupations. Demand outstrips supply, and the government allocates status through a random lottery. In September 2025, The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposed a new lottery process that would weight applications favoring workers receiving higher wage offers. This short article demonstrates that a weighted lottery would increase the ethnic diversity of H-1B recipients. Implications for H-1B employment concentration are particularly sensitive to threshold cutoffs used to construct weights.

title: Project Selection, Planning and Execution: A Review
affiliations: , Ohio State University (OSU) - Department of Management Sciences and Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University

detail.title: Project Selection, Planning and Execution: A Review
detail.abstract: About 30% of the world's economic activity is managed as projects. Yet many projects fail to meet expectations for time, cost, and quality of deliverables. To understand why this is the case and identify possible solutions, this paper offers a structured review of recent project management research. We examine the project selection, planning, and execution stages from both descriptive and prescriptive perspectives. From a descriptive viewpoint, factors influencing project performance are systematically categorized into project context, organizational context, and external environmental factors. Complementarily, the prescriptive perspective provides actionable guidance for addressing challenges specific to each stage. We also review the data and methods employed across the literature. Building on these perspectives, opportunities for future research at each stage are identified. In general, this study equips project managers and researchers with a structured roadmap to understand challenges, identify appropriate tools, and effectively implement projects.

title: Quality Upgrading in Global Supply Chains: Evidence from Colombian Coffee
affiliations: University of Warwick, University of Toulouse 1 - Toulouse School of Economics (TSE), Universidad de los Andes - Department of Economics, Columbia University - School of International & Public Affairs (SIPA), University of Basel and Columbia University

detail.title: Quality Upgrading in Global Supply Chains: Evidence from Colombian Coffee

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Do the returns to quality upgrading pass through supply chains to primary producers? We explore this question in the context of Colombia’s coffee sector, in which market outcomes depend on interactions between farmers, exporters (which operate mills), and international buyers, and contracts are for the most part not legally enforceable. We formalize the hypothesis that quality upgrading is subject to a key hold-up problem: producing highquality beans requires long-term investments by farmers, but there is no guarantee that an exporter will pay a quality premium when the beans arrive at its mills. An international buyer with sufficient demand for high-quality coffee can solve this problem by imposing a vertical restraint on the exporter, requiring the exporter to pay a quality premium to farmers. Combining internal records from two exporters, comprehensive administrative data, and the staggered rollout of a buyer-driven quality-upgrading program, we find empirical support for the key theoretical predictions. The results are consistent with the hypotheses that quality upgrading can provide a path to higher incomes for farmers, but also that it is unlikely to be viable under standard market conditions in the sector.

title: Growing from the STEM? OPT Classification and International Students in Economics
affiliations: Iowa State University and Iowa State University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Growing from the STEM? OPT Classification and International Students in Economics

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: The Optional Practical Training (OPT) program now provides up to 36 months of employment authorization for foreign students completing college degrees in the U.S. in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) fields. Econometrics and Quantitative Economics (EQE) was added as a STEM field in 2012, triggering an explosion of EQE programs and degrees conferred, but some of this growth involved displacement from other economics programs. We document the growth of EQE and examine effects of OPT and EQE program creation on overall economics bachelors degrees conferred to international students. We find positive effects on international economics degrees with effects that appear larger at public colleges and universities than private ones. We also examine effects on domestic students and find more mixed results. Our results suggest that EQE program creation on average benefits foreign students and higher education institutions.

title: Racial and Gendered Impacts of International Students on Domestic Peers
affiliations: University of Colorado at Boulder - Department of Economics, Hamilton College and

detail.title: Racial and Gendered Impacts of International Students on Domestic Peers

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of international students on the academic outcomes of domestic peers in introductory economics courses. We address the potential endogeneity of class selection by focusing on first-year students enrolling in a large public flagship university, for whom class assignment is likely to be quasi-random, conditional on a rich set of control variables for the class and individual. Results suggest an increased share of international student peers reduces the likelihood of majoring in economics for domestic White and Asian men while increasing the likelihood of majoring in economics for domestic men from underrepresented racial and ethnic groups. There is also evidence that higher shares of international student peers increase the likelihood that domestic White and Asian men major in business and decrease the likelihood that some men drop out of college. Additional analyses point to introductory course grades as possible mechanisms to explain these results, as a higher international peer share is associated with higher domestic student grades. Results for men enrolled in large introductory economics classes are similar to the main results for men overall and are also similar for women.

title: Consumption Patterns, Inflation, and Household Welfare: Demand-Based Equivalence Scales in Europe
affiliations: Institute of Economics, Zagreb, Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research (LISER), Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research (LISER), University of Verona - Department of Economics and University of Galway

detail.title: Consumption Patterns, Inflation, and Household Welfare: Demand-Based Equivalence Scales in Europe

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Equivalence scales are central to distributional analysis, adjusting household incomes for size and composition and shaping poverty and inequality measurement. Despite changes in consumption patterns, most applied work continues to rely on the modified OECD scale from the 1990s. We revisit equivalence scales for 23 EU countries using a linear expenditure demand system and harmonized Household Budget Survey data for 2010–2020. We estimate three demand-based scales: a minimum-needs scale anchored in subsistence, a utility-implicit scale based on welfare equivalence under common preferences, and a utility-explicit scale for sensitivity analysis. Our estimates imply larger economies of scale than the modified OECD scale, particularly for larger households. Scales decline with living standards and over time. Simulations of 2020–2024 price changes suggest that recent inflation is likely to further reduce equivalence scales, with stronger effects for households with children. While regional heterogeneity remains, poverty measures are more sensitive than inequality measures to the choice of scale. The results highlight the need to update equivalence scales and to report distributional statistics under alternative assumptions.

title: The Effect of Separation on Poverty and Employment

detail.title: The Effect of Separation on Poverty and Employment

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using 2001–2021 HILDA survey data, this paper estimates how separation or divorce affects poverty and employment trajectories over five years after the event. A difference-in-differences approach compares separated individuals with couples who stayed together, accounting for recent and long-term labour market history prior to separation. Women with preschool children face a 19.9 percentage point higher poverty risk in the first year, which fades within three years. Women with older or no children experience smaller but longer-lasting poverty increases. Preseparation employment strongly moderates effects: non-employed women face much higher poverty risks than employed women who have similar poverty risks to men. Men’s poverty impacts are smaller and shorter-lived. Separation barely changes women’s employment but slightly reduces men’s employment, especially those with preschool children.

title: How Home Exams and Peers Affect College Grades in Unprecedented Times
affiliations: University of Iceland, University of Essex, University of Iceland and University of Iceland

detail.title: How Home Exams and Peers Affect College Grades in Unprecedented Times

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Leveraging administrative data from the University of Iceland, which cover more than 60% of the undergraduate population in the country, we examine how home exams and peer networks shape grades around the COVID-19 crisis. Using difference-in-difference models with a rich set of fixed effects, we find that home exams taken during university closures raised grades by about 0.5 points (about 7%) relative to invigilated in-person exams outside the pandemic period. Access to a larger share of high-school peers leads to an average grade increase of up to two-fifths of a point, and exposure to higher-quality peers yielded additional, but smaller gains. Interactions between peer-network measures and the COVID/home-exam indicators are near zero, providing no evidence that peer networks amplified home-exam gains during the pandemic.

title: Supported Work Leads to Lasting Labor Market Success Among TANF Recipients
affiliations: University of Colorado at Boulder - Department of Economics, University of Colorado at Boulder - Department of Economics and University of Notre Dame

detail.title: Supported Work Leads to Lasting Labor Market Success Among TANF Recipients

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies the effects of a supported work program that provides TANF recipients with a suite of services including a six-month subsidized internship with a local employer.  We use rich administrative data and implement a stacked difference-in-differences design comparing program participants to observably similar TANF recipients to estimate effects on employment, earnings, and benefit receipt. Program enrollment led to an immediate increase in formal-sector employment and earnings, with limited post-program fadeout. The program increased employment by 10 percentage points (20 percent) and earnings by \$861 per quarter (48 percent) in the three years following program exit. Program participation also increased participants' total benefit receipt during the program, with modest decreases after program exit.  The program is relatively cost-effective compared to other adult subsidized employment programs due to longer-than-average persistence of the employment and earnings gains.

title: The Politics of Public Service Reform

detail.title: The Politics of Public Service Reform

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper provides experimental evidence on the electoral effect of a large education reform in a developing democracy. The reform significantly improved school quality on many dimensions (Romero, Sandefur, & Sandholtz, 2020). In this paper, I show that the reform reduced the incumbent party's pres- idential vote share by 2.1 percentage points (5%). The reform also reduced teachers' job satisfaction, support for the incumbent government, and political engagement. Electoral effects were positively correlated with effects on teachers' political engagement; the reform lost most votes where it caused greatest political disengagement of teachers.

title: The Minimum Wage and Inequality Between Groups
affiliations: Cornell University - Department of Economics, , Cornell University, Cornell University - School of Industrial and Labor Relations and Cornell University

detail.title: The Minimum Wage and Inequality Between Groups

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using 1979-2019 Current Population Survey data, we study the effect of state and federal minimum wage policies on gender, race, and ethnic inequality. We find that minimum wages substantially reduce intergroup wage inequality at least up to the 20th wage percentile, with no evidence of adverse employment effects. We conduct counterfactual simulations of between- group inequality due to minimum wage changes since 1979. Declines in the real minimum wage in the 1980s slowed progress in narrowing between-group inequality. Relatively small changes in minimum wages during 1989-1998 and 1998-2007 meant little role for the minimum wage over those time spans. Since 2007, several states have steeply raised their minimum wages, especially raising Hispanics’ relative wages, because they earn low wages and reside disproportionately in those states. Finally, we find that raising the federal minimum wage to $12/hour in 2020 dollars ($14.49 in 2025Q2 dollars) would reduce existing between-group wage gaps below the 15th percentile by 25-50%.

title: Matching or Clashing: Exploring Scientists Exit from Academia Through Intentions and Job Offers
affiliations: ,  and The University of Manchester - Alliance Manchester Business School

detail.title: Matching or Clashing: Exploring Scientists Exit from Academia Through Intentions and Job Offers

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Academically trained scientists play a pivotal role in innovation by advancing the knowledge frontier across industries, prompting firms to increasingly engage in proactive recruitment. This paper investigates academic scientists’ career transitions into industry by jointly examining two often separately studied mechanisms: scientists’ intentions to leave academia (the supply side) and firms’ recruitment efforts (the demand side). We conceptualize intersectoral mobility as the outcome of how these two mechanisms align or diverge. Using survey data from 469 scientists in Germany linked to follow-up information on their actual career outcomes more than three years later, our results show that exit intentions are the predominant predictor of subsequent transitions into industry jobs. Job offers reinforce the impact of existing exit intentions. By contrast, scientists who receive a job offer but do not intend to leave academia are the least likely to transition to private-sector employment. Implications for firms’ active recruiting strategies and for universities seeking to retain scientific staff are discussed.

title: War and the Economy: Do Post-war Economies Recover Stronger or Weaker?

detail.title: War and the Economy: Do Post-war Economies Recover Stronger or Weaker?
detail.abstract: War has traditionally been among the most dislocative yet creative drivers of world economies. Although wars typically lead to destruction, exile, and chronic instability, recoveries in the aftermath of war have had surprisingly varied results across countries. This paper examines whether economies recover more or less robustly following wars through comparative case studies in Germany and Japan after World War II and Iraq after 2003. Employing a mixed-method framework integrating historical economic statistics, trends in GDP growth, and cross-disciplinary knowledge from economics, political science, and sociology, the research draws attention to how institutional reconstruction, foreign assistance, and governance frameworks shape recovery patterns. Evidence indicates that short-term economic downturn is unavoidable, but countries with reconstructive policies that are inclusive, robust governance, and international partnership will likely have "war-induced modernization," such as that in Japan and Germany. However, countries with weak institutions and poor governance, like Iraq, experience lasting economic stagnation. The study emphasizes that war itself is not necessarily an economic "bounty" but a conditional disruptor: its effects are conditional on governance, external alliances, and the inclusiveness of recovery policies. The report concludes that postwar economies need to implement sustainable, human-oriented policies that emphasize innovation, social fairness, and regional collaboration to prevent cycle-back violence and economic breakdown. This study also suggests imminent policy direction including "green reconstruction funds," digital-first programs for recovery, and collaborative regional trade agreements to ensure recovery is not just speedy but also resilient.

title: Who Studies What? Country of Origin, Gender, and Field Specialization Among Economics PhDs
affiliations: University of Luxembourg and LISER

detail.title: Who Studies What? Country of Origin, Gender, and Field Specialization Among Economics PhDs

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the determinants of field specialization among U.S. economics PhD students, focusing on individual, institutional, and contextual factors shaping early research careers. Using data on over 8,000 dissertations from 2009–2018, we classify each dissertation into one of ten fields using author-reported JEL codes and topic modeling of abstracts. We link dissertations to student gender, program characteristics, and country of origin inferred from surnames and matched to country-level indicators. We find substantial variation in field choice by region of origin. Gender gaps in specialization are not uniform but vary in size and direction across regions, indicating that gender and origin interact in shaping choices. Results are robust to alternative classification methods and to using genetic distance as a continuous measure of origin. Our findings highlight how early specialization in economics reflects inherited context and institutional exposure, with implications for research agendas, job market outcomes, and diversity across subfields.

title: From Division of Labour to Division of Intelligence: Rethinking Jobs, Skills, and Workforce Planning in the AI Era

detail.title: From Division of Labour to Division of Intelligence: Rethinking Jobs, Skills, and Workforce Planning in the AI Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming not only who does work, but how intelligence itself is divided between humans and machines. Building on Adam Smith's (1776) theory of the division of labour and Jordan's (2025) collectivist economic perspective on AI, it develops a neo-Smithian framework for the 'division of intelligence' in modern organisations. Rather than treating AI as a jobdestroying force or a simple augmentation tool, the analysis emphasises that AI reshapes work by redistributing tasks, judgment, and decision rights across humanmachine systems. The paper identifies four broad categories of tasks-AI-first, human-first, and two forms of hybrid work-and proposes design principles for allocating work according to the distinctive strengths of humans and AI. Evidence from healthcare, finance, education, and the HR function itself illustrates how these patterns play out in practice. Five critical competency areas are highlighted for workers in an AI-enabled economy, and a dedicated section translates the framework into concrete implications for HR, job design, and workforce planning. Ethical analysis, grounded in the principles of beneficence, non-maleficence, autonomy, and justice (Beauchamp & Childress, 2019), underscores that efficiency and ethics are not competing goals but jointly define what 'good' looks like in AIenabled systems. The central thesis is that success in the AI era depends on deliberately designing collaborative human-machine systems in which each contributes their unique strengths-and in which organisations treat AI deployment as workforce and system redesign, not just technology installation.

title: Public Insurance and Demand for Private Healthcare
affiliations: University of Warwick, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur and City College of New York

detail.title: Public Insurance and Demand for Private Healthcare

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Establishment of public–private partnerships is an emerging model in health care delivery. This study evaluates a pioneering social health insurance program in India that enables eligible households to access private hospitals for tertiary care services free of cost, but does not build more facilities. Leveraging policy discontinuities at state borders, we identify the program’s causal effects on utilization of private facilities and associated out-of-pocket expenditures. The results indicate a pronounced substitution effect induced by relative price changes: the program substantially increases the incidence of deliveries in private hospitals while significantly reducing out-of-pocket spending. However, we find no statistically significant effects on fertility or a key health outcome, infant mortality.

detail.abstract:
Sustainability has become a critical driver of strategic competitiveness, yet many firms continue to struggle with implementation. Regulatory advances in the European Union-most notably the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), and the 2024-2025 Omnibus Package-have accelerated adoption, but regulation alone is insufficient to enable transformation. 
This paper introduces the concept of a Culture of Sustainability, defined as a shared organizational mindset that embeds long-term thinking, multi-stakeholder value creation, and systemic awareness across the enterprise. Building on organizational culture theory (Schein, 1992; Hofstede, 2001) 1 , corporate purpose research (Gartenberg, Prat, & Serafeim, 2019) 2 , and the integrated thinking framework (IIRC, 2013) 3 , the study presents a three-pillar model-Purpose, Leadership, and Culture-to explain how sustainability can evolve from compliance to strategic differentiation. The analysis suggests that strict regulation drives compliance, while simplified regulation reveals leadership. Only organizations with a mature Culture of Sustainability are able to align strategy and behavior, foster innovation, and build resilience. The findings offer a conceptual roadmap for business leaders seeking to embed sustainability into core practices and organizational identity.

detail.title: Assortative Mating, Inequality, and Rising Educational Mobility in Spain

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the evolution of intergenerational educational mobility and related distributional statistics in Spain. Over recent decades, mobility has risen by one-third, coinciding with pronounced declines in inequality and assortative mating among the same cohorts. To explore these patterns, we examine regional correlates of mobility, using split-sample techniques. A key finding from both national and regional analyses is the close association between mobility and assortative mating: spousal sorting accounts for nearly half of the regional variation in intergenerational correlations and also appears to be a key mediator of the negative relationship between inequality and mobility documented in recent studies.

title: The 'Despotic Leviathan' and Its Financial Architecture: How IMF Conditionalities Deepen Inequality
affiliations: University of Bath and

detail.title: The 'Despotic Leviathan' and Its Financial Architecture: How IMF Conditionalities Deepen Inequality

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines how IMF policies contribute to the inequality in MENA, and to a Middle-Income Trap (MIT). Developing a theory expanding Acemoglu and Robinson’s “Narrow Corridor” framework, it shows how IMF conditions align domestic elite incentives with creditor interests through a principal-agent lens. Using 2020-2025 data, its analysis reveals IMF monetary policies create rent-seeking structures that institutionalize inequality and suppress growth. The paper identifies an “engineered r>g dynamic” as a quantifiable signature of this extraction, empirically verified in Egypt. It establishes a causal link between financial/monetary policy (interest rates, debt compounding) and the “Despotic Leviathan” state formation.

title: An Application to Latin America of a Dual Synergies Model: Can a New Industrial Policy Break the Middle Income Trap?
affiliations: University of Bath

detail.title: An Application to Latin America of a Dual Synergies Model: Can a New Industrial Policy Break the Middle Income Trap?

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: The paper applies the “dual synergies” model—linking economic growth, poverty reduction, and human capability formation—to explain why Latin America (LAC) remains trapped at middle-income levels. It challenges orthodox views that prioritize growth alone, arguing instead that growth, social policy, and human capital mutually reinforce each other. Using stylized facts, the paper shows that LAC’s extractive, commodity-dependent development model has produced volatile growth, weak job creation, high informality, and limited poverty reduction. This contrasts sharply with East Asia, where coordinated industrial policy, early investments in health and education, and financial deepening enabled sustained growth and structural transformation. In LAC, weak fiscal capacity, low savings, foreign-dominated banking, and inequality constrain public investment in human capital, weakening growth–poverty links. The paper argues that breaking the middle-income trap requires an integrated strategy: a renewed, state-capable industrial policy aimed at diversification, innovation, and manufacturing upgrading, combined with stronger social policies.

title: Crime and Prices: Evidence from Thefts of Expensive Precious Metal
affiliations: Singapore Management University, London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP) and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP)

detail.title: Crime and Prices: Evidence from Thefts of Expensive Precious Metal

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study whether economic incentives matter for crime in a novel way, through study of expensive precious metal thefts by thieves stealing catalytic converters. We combine sharp, plausibly exogenous variation in the prices of precious metals embedded in converters with newly assembled U.S. data and multiple research designs. We show that phenomenally fast increases in precious metal prices generated a sizeable and rapid rise in auto-part thefts, while subsequent price declines and policy responses quickly reversed this pattern. The resulting boom-and-bust dynamics provide clean evidence that both demand- and supply-side economic forces shape property crime and inform targeted deterrence policies.

title: Why Is Competition in the European Football Market Failing, and What Should Be Done About It?
affiliations: Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN) and Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN)

detail.title: Why Is Competition in the European Football Market Failing, and What Should Be Done About It?

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: The European football (soccer) market increasingly funnels rents to superstar players and intermediaries while weakening competitive balance. We trace this dynamic to two forces: (a) technological innovation that globalized broadcasting and magnified superstar returns, and (b) legal rulings boosting player mobility and causing bidding wars. The 2024 Diarra ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union further loosens transfer constraints and will likely intensify talent concentration at “superclubs”. The result is soaring salaries and transfer fees, persistent financial fragility among non-elite clubs, and growing predictability of match outcomes. We evaluate reform options that preserve Europe’s open-league tradition yet borrow from North American competitive-balance tools: greater revenue sharing, hard/soft salary caps, and draft-like mechanisms. These should be complemented by a “cartel tax” to fund youth sport, and club-governance codes plus credible financial-sustainability rules.

title: Formal and Informal Assets in the Italian Labour Market
affiliations: , Università degli Studi di Milano - Dipartimento di Economia Politica e Aziendale (DEPA),  and University College London, Institute of Education

detail.title: Formal and Informal Assets in the Italian Labour Market

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper estimates labour-market returns to formal and informal human capital in Italy using data from the first cycle of PIAAC. We distinguish formal inputs (years of schooling) from directly assessed skills (literacy and numeracy) which we interpret as distinct forms of human capital that are shaped by school quality and by non-formal and informal learning. To address non-random employment and joint endogeneity of schooling and skills, we combine a Heckman selection model with instrumental variables. Schooling is instrumented using cohort exposure to the 1971 introduction of full-day primary schooling and the 1999–2001 Bologna ‘3+2’ university reform; skills are instrumented using gender- and cohort-specific municipal illiteracy rates from population censuses, matched by birthplace. Results show that ignoring selection and endogeneity overstates the returns to schooling. After correction, numeracy yields the main wage premium, while formal credentials contribute little once skills are accounted for. The findings highlight the role of early cultural environments and skill accumulation for Italian wage inequality in Italy.

title: Gutenberg or the Great Firewall? Printing, AI, and the Politics of Innovation
affiliations: Harvard University

detail.title: Gutenberg or the Great Firewall? Printing, AI, and the Politics of Innovation
detail.abstract: This paper examines the potential of the two frontrunners-the United States and China-for long-run AI leadership. It develops a simple model of sustained innovation in information technologies, arguing that long-run progress hinges on "governed Schumpeterian competition": strong but constrained state capacity combined with Schumpeterian entrepreneurship that sustains creative destruction. Using the historical experience of the printing press-an early information technology with disruptive features analogous to AI-the paper shows how different institutional endowments shape the trajectory of these technologies. In imperial China, competition was initially imported via Buddhism but was later absorbed into a centralized, stability-first order, while in fragmented Western Europe, low exit costs and competition allowed printing to evolve. The analysis then applies this lens to AI, comparing the political economy of the U.S. and China to examine how each system structurally approaches AI development and innovation. While the U.S. still leads, China's model constitutes a major institutional innovation, combining a state-capitalist system with Schumpeterian entrepreneurship. Although it remains unclear whether it has solved the autocrats' dilemma between stability and creative destruction, China could be capable of overtaking the U.S. in AI over the long run.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the growing impact of artificial intelligence, particularly deepfake technologies, on the integrity and reliability of the audit process. It examines how increasingly sophisticated AI-generated media can be used to fabricate evidence, elevating the risk of fraud and challenging auditors’ ability to verify the authenticity of digital information. The paper explains the mechanisms behind deepfake creation, such as generative adversarial networks, to illustrate why these forgeries are becoming more difficult to detect. It further assesses the tools currently available to auditors, including deepfake-detection algorithms, large training datasets, and watermarking techniques, as potential safeguards against manipulated evidence. In addition, the study evaluates emerging global legislative responses and highlights the present lack of comprehensive regulation surrounding AI misuse. While emphasizing the significant threats deepfakes pose to audit quality, the paper also acknowledges the constructive applications of AI that can enhance efficiency, accuracy, and analytical capabilities in auditing. Ultimately, the study underscores the need for a combined strategy of technology adoption, regulatory development, and auditor education to address the evolving risks posed by AI-generated misinformation.

title: Understanding Paradigm Resistance: Why Innovative Wave-Mechanics Papers Are Misread as Redundant Attacks on Impedance Matching Theory
